item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating evidence relevance, claim support, and evidence sufficiency. A 2025 protocol labels relevance first, then distinguishes support/refutation from several insufficient-evidence states; its authors report improved agreement from these finer distinctions ([study](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.968.pdf)). Another 2025 rubric explicitly prioritizes acknowledging insufficient references and explaining what is missing ([abstention guidelines](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.877.pdf)). ACORN (2024) evaluates explanations by separate quality aspects and finds that substituting LLM ratings often reduces human agreement—automated diagnostic annotations need calibration against human judgments ([ACORN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04818)). These are transferable methods, not a validated Amazon recommendation rubric.\n\nFor the twenty training users, an adapted recommendation-level record should contain candidate ID, linked history item IDs/timestamps, exact title/description evidence, label, and uncertainty reason. Annotate separately: specific recent connection; apparent duplication with a named history or recommendation item; explicit textual compatibility support or contradiction; insufficient information. Define recency beforehand. Similar titles support apparent duplication, not confirmed ownership; history interactions do not establish intent or satisfaction. Compatibility requires explicit matching requirements/specifications; missing details warrant abstention. Pilot the rubric, independently double-annotate recommendations, retain original judgments before adjudication, and report per-label agreement, abstention rates, label counts, and uncertainty intervals clustered by user. A 2026 review emphasizes matching agreement measures to annotation design and intended interpretation ([Counting on Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06865)). Treat these annotations as evidence audits, not measured user satisfaction or substitutes for validation HR@10."}
